title: The Expansions, Part 1: The Burning Crusade
summary_html:
Season 2 opens with The Burning Crusade (2007): the BlizzCon 2005 reveal and the slip into January 2007, a record 2.4 million copies sold in a day, blood elves and draenei, Outland and Shattrath, flying mounts, Karazhan and the end of 40-player raiding, Nihilum's world-first run to Illidan, the Sunwell and Kil'jaeden, arenas and the first Arena tournament, reviews and Metacritic, the 2007 community stories, and the expansion's two Classic returns in 2021 and 2026.

  • Reveal: Announced at the first BlizzCon (October 28, 2005); blood elves first, draenei about six months later.
  • Delay: Moved from November 2006 to January 2007 to extend beta; minimum connection rose to broadband.
  • Launch: January 16, 2007; about 4 million copies shipped to 5,000+ stores; 2.4 million sold in 24 hours; 1.7 million upgraded on day one.
  • Subscribers: Nearly 8.5 million by March 2007, 9 million by July, 9.3 million by November.
  • Story: Illidan, Kael'thas and Vashj in Outland; the naaru M'uru and the Blood Knights; the Sunwell restored by Velen.
  • Raids: Karazhan as the first 10-player raid; new raids capped at 25 (Ion Hazzikostas on why); patch 2.4 badge gear and attunement removal.
  • World firsts: Nihilum took Gruul through Illidan and Archimonde in 2007; SK Gaming killed Kil'jaeden in May 2008 after 62 days.
  • Systems: Level 70, combat ratings and resilience, jewelcrafting and sockets, cross-faction paladins and shamans, flying in Outland.
  • Arena: Three arenas and the Swift Nether Drake; BlizzCon 2007 tournament won by MoB Turtlebeach ($25,000 of a $40,000 pool).
  • Reception: Metascore 91 (46 critics); GameRankings about 90%; GamesRadar 9/10; GamePro 5/5; GameSpot praise and gripes.
  • Classic: Burning Crusade Classic (June 1, 2021, with the Dark Portal Pass and cloning-fee backlash); Sunwell cleared in about 52 minutes in 2022; the 2026 Anniversary Edition and its changes.

title: Azeroth Unearthed, Part 7: The Business of Azeroth
summary_html:
Part Seven follows the money. Alder and Pip trace World of Warcraft's subscriber curve from launch to the twelve million peak in October 2010 and the 2015 decision to stop reporting, the ownership chain from Davidson and Vivendi through the 2008 Activision merger and the 2013 buyback, the long China saga with The9 and NetEase, gold farming and the Glider bot case, the Celestial Steed and the WoW Token, the 2021 California lawsuit and workplace reckoning, and Microsoft's 2023 acquisition, layoffs and the 2024 union.

  • The peak: Blizzard announced 12 million subscribers on October 7, 2010, with a definition that counted internet game room players active in the last 30 days.
  • The blackout: After a 5.5 million report for September 30, 2015, Activision Blizzard stopped disclosing subscriber numbers.
  • Ownership: Davidson, CUC, Cendant, Havas and Vivendi, then the $18.9 billion Activision Blizzard merger (July 10, 2008) and the $8.2 billion buyback from Vivendi (2013).
  • China: The9's 2005 launch with pay by the hour, the 2009 NetEase handover and nearly three months offline, the GAPP and Ministry of Culture dispute, the January 2023 shutdown and the August 1, 2024 return.
  • Gold farming: Julian Dibbell's 2007 New York Times Magazine report and Richard Heeks' estimate of 400,000+ workers in Asia.
  • Bots in court: MDY v. Blizzard, the Glider case, and the Ninth Circuit's mixed December 2010 ruling.
  • Monetization: The Celestial Steed queue (April 2010), the WoW Token (April 2015) and its Battle.net Balance option (February 2017), and the $15 US price unchanged since 2004.
  • Reckoning: The July 2021 California lawsuit, walkouts and leadership departures, the November 2021 WSJ report, and the $54 million settlement (December 2023).
  • Microsoft: The $68.7 billion acquisition closed October 13, 2023, followed by 1,900 job cuts in January 2024 and the World of Warcraft Game Makers Guild union in July 2024.
  • For Glurp Glurp: Why gold-seller whispers are a twenty-year-old story, and a word on space horses.

title: The Expansions, Part 2: Wrath of the Lich King
summary_html:
Part 2 heads to Northrend for Wrath of the Lich King (2008): the BlizzCon 2007 reveal and the dance studio that never came, the zombie plague, a record 2.8 million copies in a day and the road to 12 million subscribers, Arthas, the Wrathgate and phasing, death knights, achievements and dual spec, Naxxramas to Ulduar to Icecrown Citadel, the Dungeon Finder, the Ensidia Saronite Bomb ban, reviews and Metacritic, and how Wrath Classic first left out the Dungeon Finder and then put it back.

  • Reveal: BlizzCon 2007 (August 3), about 13,000 attendees; death knight as the first hero class; Arthas narrates the trailer.
  • Dance studio: Listed as a feature in 2007, "still on the list" for years, never shipped.
  • Pre-launch: Patch 3.0.2 (October 14, 2008) turned on achievements; the zombie plague event began October 22.
  • Launch: November 13, 2008; 15,000+ midnight stores; 2.8 million sold in 24 hours; 4 million+ in the first month; 11.5 million subscribers by December 2008.
  • Peak: 12 million subscribers announced October 7, 2010, after Wrath reached mainland China (August 31, 2010).
  • Story: The Wrathgate, the Battle for the Undercity, phasing in Icecrown, the Lich King's fall and Bolvar's crown.
  • Systems: Death knights, achievements, vehicles, barbershop, inscription and glyphs, heirlooms, dual spec, 10- and 25-player raids.
  • Raids: Ensidia's quick Naxxramas clear; Ulduar's hard modes, Algalon and Stars' Alone in the Dark; Trial of the Crusader criticism; Paragon's heroic Lich King.
  • Exploits: Exodus suspended over Yogg-Saron (2009); Ensidia's Saronite Bomb Lich King kill revoked (February 2010).
  • Patch 3.3: Icecrown Citadel and the cross-realm Dungeon Finder (December 8, 2009).
  • Reception: Metascore 91 (47 critics); GameSpot praise and gripes; GamesRadar's "more of the same."
  • Classic: Launched September 26, 2022 without the Dungeon Finder; reversed in 2023 and added with patch 3.4.3; China launch June 27, 2024.

title: The Expansions, Part 3: Cataclysm
summary_html:
Alder and Pip dig into Cataclysm (2010), the expansion that remade the original world: the BlizzCon 2009 reveal, Tom Chilton's GDC account of rebuilding Azeroth, Christie Golden's The Shattering and Garrosh's rise, Deathwing's random sky attacks, the record launch, the punishing heroics, the talent and archaeology post-mortems, Firelands and Dragon Soul, transmog and Raid Finder, the subscriber slide and the Annual Pass, and the surprise of Cataclysm Classic in 2024.

  • Announced: August 21, 2009 at BlizzCon; the Shattering patch 4.0.3a went live November 23, 2010.
  • Launch: December 7, 2010; over 3.3 million sold in 24 hours and 4.7 million in the first month, per Blizzard.
  • Peak: Blizzard reported more than 12 million subscribers before launch.
  • Design: Chilton's GDC 2011 talk on the one-third approach to remaking zones, with Westfall and Desolace as examples.
  • Post-mortems: Blizzard's 2012 retrospectives admitted heroics were overtuned, talents disappointed and archaeology was too grindy.
  • Patches: Firelands (4.2, June 28, 2011) and Hour of Twilight (4.3, November 29, 2011) with Dragon Soul, Raid Finder, transmogrification and void storage.
  • World firsts: Paragon took heroic Sinestra and heroic 25-player Ragnaros.
  • Reception: Metascore 90 from 53 critics; user score 5.8.
  • Business: subscriptions fell to 10.3 million by November 2011; the Annual Pass offered a free copy of Diablo III.
  • Classic: Cataclysm Classic was announced at BlizzCon 2023 and launched May 20, 2024, with changes such as no guild leveling.

title: The Expansions, Part 4: Mists of Pandaria
summary_html:
Alder and Pip tell the story of Mists of Pandaria (2012): pandaren from Samwise Didier's sketches and a 2002 April Fools joke to BlizzCon 2011's mocked reveal, the launch and sales, the continent and the Sha, the overhaul of talents, monks, scenarios, challenge modes and pet battles, the daily-quest grind, Landfall, the Thunder King and Siege of Orgrimmar, Method's world firsts (including the BlizzCon 2013 live race), Garrosh's fall and trial, the subscriber slide and the 14-month drought, and the reappraisal through Remix (2024) and Mists of Pandaria Classic (2025).

  • Origins: pandaren started as Didier's art and a 2002 April Fools joke, joined The Frozen Throne, and were swapped for draenei during Burning Crusade development.
  • Announced: October 21, 2011 at BlizzCon; Chris Metzen insisted the pandaren were "not a joke."
  • Launch: September 25, 2012 (China October 2); about 2.7 million sold in week one; over 10 million subscribers.
  • Systems: monk class, six-tier talents, scenarios, challenge modes, pet battles, Sunsong Ranch, account-wide collections, AoE looting.
  • Patches: Landfall (Nov 27, 2012), Rise of the Thunder King (Mar 5, 2013), Escalation (May 21, 2013), Siege of Orgrimmar (Sep 10, 2013) with Flexible raiding and the Timeless Isle.
  • Race to world first: Method beat everyone to Ra-den and heroic Garrosh, then won the live race against Midwinter at BlizzCon 2013.
  • Story: Tides of War and Theramore, the Sha and Y'Shaarj, Vol'jin's rebellion, and Garrosh's trial in War Crimes (2014).
  • Reception: Metascore 82 from 42 critics; user score 5.8.
  • Business: subscriptions fell from 9.6 million at the start of 2013 to 7.6 million by Q3 2013; Warlords did not arrive until November 13, 2014.
  • Legacy: Remix: Mists of Pandaria (May 16 to August 20, 2024) and Mists of Pandaria Classic (launched July 21, 2025).

title: The Expansions, Part 5: Warlords of Draenor
summary_html:
Part Five of The Expansions covers Warlords of Draenor (2014): Garrosh's time-travel escape and the uncorrupted Iron Horde, the Lords of War shorts, a record-adjacent launch of 3.3 million day-one sales and a rebound above 10 million subscribers, the queue- and DDoS-plagued first week and J. Allen Brack's apology, superb leveling and raids, the lonely garrison, the 6.1 "selfie patch", the no-flying reversal and Draenor Pathfinder, the fall to 5.6 million subscribers, the Archimonde ending that set up Legion, and why there is still no Warlords Classic.

  • Reveal and release: announced at BlizzCon on November 8, 2013; launched November 13, 2014 (Asia regions November 20).
  • Launch numbers: over 3.3 million copies sold in 24 hours; subscribers back above 10 million, up from 7.7 million.
  • Rocky start: overcrowded realms and a launch-day DDoS; five free days of game time and an apology from J. Allen Brack.
  • Systems: level 100, garrisons and followers, new character models, item squish, hit/expertise removed, Toy Box, near-instant server batching.
  • Raids: Highmaul, Blackrock Foundry and the 13-boss Hellfire Citadel ending with Archimonde.
  • The drought: 6.1 (Feb 24, 2015) brought selfies and Twitter; 6.2 (June 23, 2015) was the last major patch; Hellfire Citadel the last raid.
  • Flying: the no-flying stance, weeks of backlash, and Ion Hazzikostas's June 10, 2015 reversal via Draenor Pathfinder.
  • Subscribers: 7.1 million in May 2015, 5.6 million in August 2015; Activision stopped reporting in November 2015.
  • Reception: Metacritic 87 from critics vs 3.9 from users; PC Gamer 90; GameSpot praised questing but faulted the garrison endgame.
  • Postmortem: Hazzikostas in 2016: "mistakes were made"; rushed schedule and too little for players with less time.
  • Classic: no Warlords Classic announced as of September 2026, per Blizzard Watch.

title: The Expansions, Part 6: Legion
summary_html:
Part Six of The Expansions covers Legion (2016), Blizzard's answer to Warlords of Draenor: the gamescom 2015 reveal two days after the 5.6 million subscriber report, the Broken Shore scenario that killed Varian and Vol'jin and made Sylvanas warchief, 3.3 million day-one sales and the best launch-week concurrency since Cataclysm, the Demon Hunter, artifacts and the Artifact Power treadmill, random legendaries and their bad-luck cap, Order Halls, world quests, the birth of Mythic Plus and the first Mythic Dungeon Invitational, Suramar, Illidan's return, Argus and Sargeras's sword, plus 2025's Legion Remix.

  • Reveal: announced August 6, 2015 at gamescom in Cologne; alpha began on the game's 11th anniversary.
  • Launch: August 30, 2016; 3.3 million sold by end of day one; highest launch-week concurrency since Cataclysm.
  • Broken Shore: Varian and Vol'jin fall; Sylvanas takes the Horde.
  • Systems: 36 artifacts, Order Halls, world quests and emissaries, zone scaling, PvP honor talents and templates, the Legion Companion app.
  • Mythic Plus: reported by Kotaku in April 2016 as Greater Rift-like; live in 7.0.3, replacing Challenge Mode; first MDI finals October 1, 2017.
  • Raids: Emerald Nightmare, Trial of Valor, Nighthold, Tomb of Sargeras, Antorus (Argus the Unmaker).
  • Pain points: random legendaries (bad luck protection soft-capped at four), the endless Artifact Power grind, titanforging.
  • Reception: PC Gamer 90 ("the most confident expansion"); Metacritic 88 critics, 7.6 users.
  • Ending: Sargeras imprisoned, Illidan his warden, the sword in Silithus and the Azerite that set up Battle for Azeroth.
  • Legacy: Legion Remix ran October 7, 2025 to January 19, 2026; no Legion Classic announced.

title: Azeroth Unearthed, Part 5: Vanilla Life
summary_html:
Pip and Alder move into Azeroth for the vanilla years, 2004 to 2006: launch queues and rollbacks, the January 2005 outage weekend and Mike Morhaime's apology, forty-player raiding from Molten Core to Naxxramas (with the bugs behind several world firsts), the Gates of Ahn'Qiraj war effort, the Southshore versus Tarren Mill wars, the brutal rank 14 honor grind, Leeroy Jenkins, the Corrupted Blood plague and the epidemiology papers it inspired, and South Park's Emmy-winning "Make Love, Not Warcraft."

  • Launch: about 240,000 copies in the first 24 hours (Nov 23, 2004), 41 realms at launch, doubled to 75 within weeks; queues of hours, loot lag and rollbacks.
  • January 2005: up to 20 of 88 servers down over the holiday weekend, Penny Arcade revokes its Game of the Year award, Blizzard credits affected players a week of free time.
  • Growth: Europe launches Feb 11, 2005; Blizzard announces 5 million customers (Dec 2005) and 6 million (early 2006), with its broad definition noted.
  • Raids: Molten Core and Onyxia at launch, Blackwing Lair (patch 1.6), Zul'Gurub (1.7), Ahn'Qiraj (1.9) and Naxxramas (1.11); Ruined, Ascent, Drama, Death and Taxes and Nihilum's world firsts.
  • Onyxia Wipe Animation: the Wipe Club recording, "50 DKP minus," and its many official callbacks.
  • World PvP: why Southshore and Tarren Mill became the game's unplanned battleground, and how battlegrounds and dishonorable kills ended its golden age.
  • Honor system: 14 ranks, weekly curve and decay, and the human cost of the rank 14 grind as told in PC Gamer's 2006 feature.
  • Leeroy Jenkins: Pals For Life on Laughing Skull, the staged Rookery pull, Jeopardy, achievements and the 2017 first take.
  • Corrupted Blood: how Hakkar's debuff escaped Zul'Gurub via pets, Blizzard's fixes, and the 2007 papers in Epidemiology and The Lancet Infectious Diseases.
  • South Park: machinima made with Blizzard's help, 3.4 million viewers and the first Emmy for machinima.
  • For Glurp Glurp: Hillsbrad, the old honor system in Forever, and staying away from hunter pets.

title: Azeroth Unearthed, Part 9: Culture and Influence
summary_html:
Part Nine of Azeroth Unearthed follows World of Warcraft out of the game and into the wider world: the Arena World Championship and Mythic Dungeon International, the accidental esport that is the Race to World First (from Nihilum's streak to Liquid's five straight world firsts in 2026), the streamers who made Classic a Twitch phenomenon, machinima and The Guild, celebrity TV ads, BlizzCon's rise, fall and 2026 return, the composers behind the score, Hearthstone, Heroes of the Storm and Warcraft Rumble, the 2016 Warcraft film, fan databases and theorycrafting, and the game's influence on design.

  • Arena esports: from the 2008 BlizzCon Arena Tournament to a Midnight Season One grand finals at BlizzCon 2026, plus Blizzard's memorial NPC for Reckful.
  • Race to World First: Nihilum's eight in a row, Method's 2018 Uldir stream that rivaled Ninja on Twitch, Complexity Limit ending Europe's streak, Echo's formation, Liquid's acquisition of Limit, and Midnight's hidden L'ura phase.
  • Mythic Dungeon International: founded 2017, renamed in 2019, the Great Push, and Echo's flawless 2021 title.
  • Streamers: Asmongold, Sodapoppin, OTK, the million viewer Classic launch, and the Olympus guild in the Forever beta.
  • Machinima and fan culture: Illegal Danish Super Snacks, Leeroy at twenty, Felicia Day's The Guild, and the "What's your game?" ads with Mr. T and William Shatner.
  • BlizzCon: four thousand attendees in 2005 to forty thousand in 2018, the cancellations, and the September 2026 return.
  • Music: Jason Hayes, Tracy W. Bush, Derek Duke, Glenn Stafford, Russell Brower and Neal Acree, and why the songs never resolve.
  • Spinoffs: Hearthstone's hundred million players, the end of Heroes of the Storm esports, and Warcraft Rumble's move to maintenance.
  • The Warcraft film: a record setting $439 million worldwide, more than half of it from China.
  • The second internet: Thottbot, Wowhead, Elitist Jerks (and the game director who came from it), and Midnight's add-on overhaul.
  • Design influence: Raph Koster's ten year retrospective, Jeff Kaplan's GDC 2009 quest talk, and Destiny's raids.
  • For Glurp Glurp: how the culture can help a level twenty-something orc frost mage.

title: The Expansions, Part 11: Midnight
summary_html:
The Expansions series ends with the one still underway. Alder and Pip cover World of Warcraft: Midnight, which launched March 2, 2026: the Worldsoul Saga announcement at BlizzCon 2023, the gamescom 2025 reveal, the long runway of alpha, beta, the December prologue and housing early access, and the fight over addon restrictions and "secret values." They also go through the rebuilt Quel'Thalas zones, player housing, the raids and new systems, the reviews, the Darkwell and Dawnwell story with its Sylvanas cliffhanger, Liquid's Race to World First win through L'ura's secret phase, and the patch year from 12.1 to 12.1.5. The episode closes on what BlizzCon 2026 confirmed about patch 12.2 Eclipse and The Last Titan, with announced facts kept clearly separate from speculation.

  • Origins: The Worldsoul Saga trilogy was announced at BlizzCon on November 3, 2023. Midnight was fully revealed at gamescom in August 2025.
  • Runway: Alpha began October 2, 2025, and beta on November 11, 2025. The prologue and housing early access arrived December 2, 2025, the Twilight Ascension pre-patch event the week of January 27, and worldwide launch on March 2, 2026. It was the first first-quarter launch since The Burning Crusade.
  • Addon restrictions: Combat data became "secret values." Deadly Boss Mods adapted, WeakAuras stepped away, and Blizzard built in its own damage meters, boss warnings and a cooldown manager.
  • Zones: Eversong Woods with a rebuilt, largely cross-faction Silvermoon, plus Zul'Aman, Harandar and the Voidstorm.
  • Housing: Homes are free, with no lottery or upkeep, and are shared across the warband. Neighborhoods have Endeavors. Critics called housing the expansion's headline feature.
  • Content: Three raids with nine bosses (The Voidspire, The Dreamrift, March on Quel'Danas) and eight dungeons. Also new: the Devourer Demon Hunter spec, the Haranir allied race, Prey, and the 40v40 battleground Slayer's Rise.
  • Reception: OpenCritic Top Critic Average of 84 (83% recommend) and a Metacritic PC Metascore of 82. IGN and Game Informer gave it 9/10, GameSpot 8/10 and PC Gamer 84.
  • Story: The Sunwell is corrupted into the Darkwell, Sylvanas returns, and the elven nations reconcile as the well becomes the Dawnwell. The hosts also cover criticism from Windows Central and a theory from Mein MMO.
  • Race to World First: L'ura had a hidden fourth phase. Liquid won on April 6 after roughly 474 pulls, edging out Echo.
  • Patch year: 12.1 Curse of Ula'tek (August 11) added the Coiled Isle, the Venomous Abyss raid and Lairs. 12.1.5 (October 13) added the Unbinding of Kith'ix raid and the Labyrinth of Kindo'jan.
  • Eclipse (12.2): Announced with a Worldcore raid, the Mantle Vault zone and Forsaken, night elf and Darkspear troll paladins. 12.2.5 drops transmog armor restrictions. The Talebound mode is due early 2027 and Wrath of the Lich King Remix in summer 2027. Eclipse has no release date yet.
  • The Last Titan: Revealed at BlizzCon 2026 with the "COLOSSAL" teaser, which shows Northrend, Icecrown and Ulduar. It is due in 2027, with a full story reveal promised for early 2027. Fan theories are labeled as theories.

title: Azeroth Unearthed, Part 1: Before the Horde
summary_html:
Part 1 of Azeroth Unearthed covers the years before the Horde. Alder and Pip follow three UCLA friends from Silicon & Synapse's porting contracts and their first console games, through the Davidson & Associates sale and the Chaos, Ogre and Blizzard name changes, to Westwood's Dune II, the Warhammer license that never happened, and the making and launch of Warcraft: Orcs & Humans in November 1994. Where sources disagree on dates, money or sales, the hosts say so.

  • Founding: Silicon & Synapse is founded by Allen Adham, Mike Morhaime and Frank Pearce (dated February 1991 or late 1990, depending on the source), with Morhaime's share borrowed from his grandmother.
  • Port years: Interplay and Brian Fargo supply conversion work, starting with Battle Chess, and Frank Pearce draws the missing One Ring for an Amiga port.
  • First originals: The Lost Vikings and Rock n' Roll Racing (1993) review well but, per Patrick Wyatt, sell poorly.
  • The sale and the name saga: Davidson & Associates buys the studio for $6.75 million in stock (February 1994). Chaos Studios hits a trademark claim, Ogre Studios is vetoed, and Blizzard comes out of a dictionary.
  • Dune II: Westwood's 1992 game sets the RTS template. It has no multiplayer, and that gap becomes Blizzard's opportunity.
  • The Warhammer question: Adham wanted a license for brand recognition. It fell through on business terms, and the team preferred to own its world. Warhammer still shaped the art.
  • Building Warcraft: Dune II art used as placeholders (and its font accidentally kept), the build button added while the bosses were at CES, box selection with a four-unit cap, the DOS extender, and the "sneaker network."
  • Multiplayer: The first match in June 1994 is a desync that both players thought they won. The team fights to keep multiplayer, and the game ships two weeks late.
  • Personality and lore: Bill Roper's improvised voices, the click gags, bright art, and the First War's lasting characters: Medivh, Lothar, Garona, Blackhand and Orgrim.
  • Launch and legacy: The game ships November 15, 1994. Sales estimates range from 100,000 to 400,000. Westwood answers with Command & Conquer, and the 2024 Remastered edition follows.
  • For Glurp Glurp: Orgrimmar's namesake, the Gurubashi trolls of Stranglethorn, and the frost spell that shares the company's name.

title: Azeroth Unearthed, Part 3: Reign of Chaos
summary_html:
Part Three of Azeroth Unearthed covers Warcraft III: how the scrapped Warcraft Legends prototype and the 1999 "role-playing strategy" reveal turned into a hero-driven RTS, why heroes, creeps and upkeep changed the genre, how the Arthas and Thrall campaigns made Warcraft a character saga, The Frozen Throne, the World Editor that produced tower defense and DotA, the early esports scene, and the 2020 Reforged backlash and its 2024 2.0 patch.

  • Origins: Warcraft Legends, Mike O'Brien's over-the-shoulder concept with no base building, dropped after about a year (Rob Pardo on Designer Notes, via Game Informer).
  • Reveal: Announced by Rob Pardo at ECTS on September 5, 1999 as a "role-playing strategy" game. Playable demons, Mana Stones and the Necromancer-builder Scourge were all cut later.
  • Launch: Released July 3, 2002. More than 4.5 million copies shipped before launch, over 1 million sold within a month, Metacritic 92, GameSpot 9.3 and Game of the Year.
  • Design: Heroes up to level 10, creeps, upkeep, day/night, and how small armies fed the esports scene (Insomnia at WCG 2003, Grubby, Moon).
  • Story: Exodus of the Horde, the Culling of Stratholme, Frostmourne, Mannoroth's death, Hyjal. Voice casting notes on Chris Metzen and Justin Gross.
  • The Frozen Throne: Released July 1, 2003. The Tavern, the Naga, Illidan, Kael'thas, Sylvanas and the Forsaken, Arthas becoming the Lich King, and the Founding of Durotar.
  • World Editor: Triggers and the object editor led to tower defense maps and Legion TD.
  • DotA: From Aeon of Strife to Eul, Guinsoo and IceFrog, then Riot, Valve, the 2012 trademark settlement and Dota 2.
  • Reforged: Metacritic 59 from critics and a record-low user score, the custom-game ownership policy, refunds, Bloomberg's 2021 report, and the November 2024 version 2.0 patch.
  • For Glurp Glurp: Durotar's origins and Grom's monument in Demon Fall Canyon, Ashenvale.

title: Azeroth Unearthed, Part 6: The Lore Codex
summary_html:
Pip and Alder unfold the cosmic map of Warcraft: the six forces from Chronicle Volume One's famous chart, titans and worldsouls, the Old Gods and the Black Empire, Sargeras and the Burning Legion, the naaru and the increasingly ambiguous Light, Azeroth revealed as a nascent titan, the Shadowlands and the First Ones, and the Worldsoul Saga through Midnight toward The Last Titan. Along the way: how the story spread across novels, manga, comics and Chronicle, Chris Metzen's departure and return, and a field guide to the franchise's retcons.

  • The chart: Light and Shadow, Life and Death, Order and Disorder, as laid out in Chronicle Volume 1 (2016), and why the Chronicle may be a biased narrator.
  • Titans: the Pantheon of Order, titans born from worldsouls, and how Chronicle and Legion reworked earlier titan lore.
  • Old Gods: Y'Shaarj, C'Thun, Yogg-Saron and N'Zoth, the Curse of Flesh, G'huun, and how each fell.
  • Sargeras and the Legion: the fall of the champion, Argus and the eredar, Medivh, and the sword in Silithus; plus the draenei retcon.
  • Azeroth the titan: hints in patch 5.3, confirmation in 7.3, Magni as Speaker, Azerite and the Heart of Azeroth, the Radiant Song.
  • The naaru: A'dal, M'uru, K'ure and Xe'ra, the darkened-naaru cycle, and disagreement about the Void.
  • Lore across media: Christie Golden's and Richard A. Knaak's novels, the Sunwell manhwa, WildStorm comics, the RPG, the magazine and the 2016 film.
  • Chris Metzen: from 1994 artist to Thrall's voice, retirement in 2016, return in 2022 and the Worldsoul Saga.
  • Shadowlands: the Arbiter, covenants, the Jailer, the Helm of Domination retcon, the First Ones, and critical reaction.
  • Worldsoul Saga: Xal'atath's rise, The War Within (2024), Midnight (March 2026) and The Last Titan (listed for 2027, TBD).
  • For Glurp Glurp: arcane on the Order corner of the chart, Thrall's voice, and the very bad real estate of Silithus.

title: The Expansions, Part 7: Battle for Azeroth
summary_html:
Part Seven of The Expansions covers Battle for Azeroth (2018): the BlizzCon 2017 reveal, the War of the Thorns and the burning of Teldrassil, a record day-one launch, Kul Tiras and Zandalar, the Heart of Azeroth and Azerite armor backlash, Warfronts and Island Expeditions, the patch arc through Visions of N'Zoth, Method and Limit in the Race to World First, the 2019 layoffs, critical versus player reception, and what lasted.

  • Announcement: Revealed at BlizzCon on November 3, 2017, alongside Allied Races, Warfronts, Island Expeditions, the Heart of Azeroth and a level 120 cap.
  • Pre-launch controversy: The War of the Thorns and the burning of Teldrassil, the Horde "shoulderless" protest for Saurfang, and Ion Hazzikostas's response.
  • Launch: Over 3.4 million units sold on the first full day, August 14, 2018, per Activision Blizzard; the first simultaneous worldwide expansion launch.
  • Zones and instances: Kul Tiras and Zandalar, ten launch dungeons plus Operation: Mechagon, and five raids from Uldir to Ny'alotha.
  • Systems: Azerite armor and the Heart of Azeroth, PC Gamer's September 2018 report on player frustration, War Mode, and the removal of First Aid.
  • Lessons: Hazzikostas's April 2019 interview on Azerite and late beta testing; Chris Kaleiki's later view that the expansion was too random.
  • Patches: Tides of Vengeance, Rise of Azshara (Essences, Nazjatar, Mechagon) and Visions of N'Zoth (Corruption, Horrific Visions).
  • Race to World First: Method's world firsts on G'huun, Jaina and Azshara, and Complexity Limit's Mythic N'Zoth, the first North American raid world first in eight years.
  • Business: Activision Blizzard's February 2019 layoffs of about eight percent of staff.
  • Reception: A Metacritic critic score of 79 next to a user score of 2.3, and OpenCritic's 77, with reviews from PC Gamer, IGN, Game Informer and others.

title: The Expansions, Part 9: Dragonflight
summary_html:
Part Nine of The Expansions covers Dragonflight (2022), the expansion that followed Shadowlands. Alder and Pip go through the April 2022 reveal and the Proletariat acquisition, then the Dracthyr Evoker, dragonriding and how it became Skyriding, and the rebuilt talents, professions and interface. They also cover launch sales (lower than Shadowlands, but better retention), the Primal Incarnates story, three raids and the Race to World First, the eight-week patch cadence, Plunderstorm, Pandaria Remix, and the critical reception.

  • Reveal: April 19, 2022. Mike Ybarra pitched a return to high fantasy roots and an overhaul of core systems.
  • Launch: pre-patch 10.0.2 in mid November 2022, expansion on November 28, 2022, level cap 70.
  • Business: early sales fell short of Shadowlands, but Western retention was higher. Blizzard had a record quarter in Q4 2022, and its games went offline in China in January 2023.
  • Dracthyr Evoker: the game's first race-and-class combination. The Augmentation support spec arrived in patch 10.1.5.
  • Dragonriding: momentum-based flight with glyphs to collect. It was renamed Skyriding in 10.2.5 and extended to almost all mounts.
  • Systems: real talent trees returned, professions got work orders and specializations, the UI got an edit mode, borrowed power and the mission table were dropped, and Mythic+ moved to rotating seasons.
  • Raids: Vault of the Incarnates (Echo world first, December 23, 2022), Aberrus (Liquid, May 15, 2023) and Amirdrassil (Echo, November 26, 2023).
  • Cadence: patches 10.0.5 through 10.2.7, with Plunderstorm (March 19, 2024) and Remix: Mists of Pandaria (May 16, 2024).
  • Reception: Metascore 82 from 26 critics, user score 3.3. PC Gamer gave it 80.
  • Legacy: merged into the base game on July 23, 2024, and the foundation for the Worldsoul Saga.

title: The Expansions, Part 10: The War Within
summary_html:
Part Ten of The Expansions covers The War Within (2024), the first chapter of the Worldsoul Saga. Alder and Pip go through the BlizzCon 2023 triple-expansion reveal, editions and early access, and the four launch zones of Khaz Algar with the Earthen. They then cover Hero Talents, Delves, Warbands and the Mythic+ changes, Xal'atath's story from the fall of Dalaran to Dimensius, three raids, and a busy patch run that included the twentieth anniversary, Siren Isle, Undermine's cars and K'aresh. The episode ends with the reviews, the player mood and the setup for Midnight.

  • Reveal: BlizzCon, November 3, 2023. The War Within, Midnight and The Last Titan were announced together as the Worldsoul Saga.
  • Launch: early access August 22 and full launch August 26, 2024. Editions cost $49.99, $69.99 and $89.99, and the level cap is 80.
  • Business: no verified sales figure is public. This was the first expansion released under Microsoft, and it was developed in parallel with the next two.
  • Hero Talents: archetype trees such as Dark Ranger, Farseer and San'layn, earned from levels 71 to 80.
  • Delves: 10 to 15 minute adventures for 1 to 5 players, with 11 tiers, Brann Bronzebeard as companion, Bountiful Coffers and the nemesis Zekvir.
  • Warbands: account-wide reputation, a shared bank, shared transmog and flight paths, added in patch 11.0.0 (July 23, 2024).
  • Story: Xal'atath destroys Dalaran, uses Ansurek and Gallywix, and takes Dimensius's power.
  • Raids: Nerub-ar Palace (September 2024), Liberation of Undermine (March 2025) and Manaforge Omega (August 2025).
  • Patches: 11.0.5 twentieth anniversary and Dracthyr class unlocks, 11.0.7 Siren Isle, 11.1 Undermine and D.R.I.V.E., 11.1.5 Nightfall and the Cooldown Manager, 11.2 Ghosts of K'aresh, 11.2.7 Skyriding skill track removed.
  • Reception: Metascore 85, with all 33 critic reviews positive. PC Gamer's January 2025 retrospective called its issues normal M M O growing pains.

title: Azeroth Unearthed, Part 2: Tides of Darkness
summary_html:
Part 2 of Azeroth Unearthed covers 1995 to 1998, when Blizzard grew from one studio with one hit into two studios with three franchises. Alder and Pip cover Warcraft II: Tides of Darkness and its Second War story, Beyond the Dark Portal, playing online through Kali and then the launch of Battle.net, Blizzard North and Diablo, StarCraft's "orcs in space" reboot, the cancelled Warcraft Adventures: Lord of the Clans, and the run of corporate owners that ended in a CUC accounting scandal.

  • Warcraft II: Work starts in early 1995 under the working title "Blood Seas" with a "land, sea and air" pitch. It adds oil, a navy, flying units, nine-unit selection, eight-player multiplayer and a map editor.
  • Second War lore: The Alliance of Lordaeron, Alterac's betrayal, the Silver Hand at Hillsbrad, Gul'dan's death knights, the enslaved red dragonflight, Lothar's death and the internment camps.
  • Sales and reviews: It debuts at No. 2 behind Myst, sells 500,000 copies in three months and about 3 million by 2001, and wins PC Gamer's Best Game of 1995.
  • Kali: An IPX emulator that put Warcraft II online. Blizzard bundled it, and Warcraft II became Kali's most popular game.
  • Beyond the Dark Portal: Blizzard pulls the contract from Cyberlore and finishes the expansion in-house (April 1996). Ner'zhul, Deathwing, and Draenor shattering into Outland.
  • Corporate soap opera: Davidson, then CUC International, then Cendant, then the 1998 CUC accounting fraud, then the sale to Havas/Vivendi.
  • Blizzard North and Diablo: Condor's turn-based design turns real-time after a team vote, and the game launches around New Year 1997.
  • Battle.net: Mike O'Brien's free service, with multiplayer added to Diablo in its last six months, then cheating, griefing, and a fast-growing user base.
  • StarCraft: Mocked at E3 1996 and reset in January 1997 with three distinct races. It ships March 31, 1998.
  • Warcraft Adventures: Thrall's first story, built with Animation Magic and voiced by Clancy Brown. It was cancelled in May 1998, leaked in 2016, and lives on in Christie Golden's novel.
  • For Glurp Glurp: Hillsbrad's Second War battlefield, and Durnholde Keep near Tarren Mill, where Thrall was held.

title: Azeroth Unearthed, Part 4: Building a World
summary_html:
Part Four of Azeroth Unearthed covers how World of Warcraft was made between 1999 and 2004. It starts with the death of Team 2's Nomad project and the plan to "make a better EverQuest," then follows the EverQuest raiders who joined the team, the design choices on death, questing, rest and add-ons, Bill Petras's art direction and John Staats's dungeons, the cut races and classes, the ECTS 2001 reveal, crunch and Allen Adham's departure, and the November 23, 2004 launch that beat Blizzard's own forecast more than tenfold.

  • Nomad to World of Warcraft: Nomad was a post-apocalyptic project inspired by Necromunda. The team voted to switch, with only the project lead against, and World of Warcraft work began two days after Nomad was scrapped in late 1999.
  • EverQuest's influence: Rob Pardo and Jeff Kaplan both came from the guild Legacy of Steel. Kaplan was hired by May 2002 as one of the first two quest designers. The faction split was inspired by Dark Age of Camelot.
  • Design pillars: A softer death penalty, quests as the main way to level, spreading players across zones, and a rest system that started in beta as an experience penalty.
  • Art and world: Bill Petras as art director, Chris Metzen making the world feel continuous, John Staats as first 3D level designer, and the Hayes, Bush, Duke and Stafford soundtrack.
  • What got cut: Around 20 candidate races, playable naga and demons, life quests, altars in place of graveyards, a level-70 layout, and the beta Water Elemental.
  • Reveal and company context: Announced at ECTS on 2 to 4 September 2001 at ExCeL London. Covers Vivendi ownership and the Blizzard North resignations of June 2003.
  • Human cost: Team 2 grew from about 40 people to hundreds under heavy crunch. Allen Adham burned out and left in 2004.
  • Launch: Released November 23, 2004. Blizzard hoped for 500,000 subscribers in the first year and had 5.6 million by December 2005. Metacritic 93, GameSpot 9.5, IGN 9.1.
  • For Glurp Glurp: Rested XP, quest routing, the missing water elemental and saving for the first mount.

title: Azeroth Unearthed, Part 8: The WoW Killers
summary_html:
Part Eight puts every so-called "WoW killer" on the table. Alder and Pip walk through EverQuest II, Vanguard, Age of Conan, Warhammer Online, Rift, Star Wars: The Old Republic, Guild Wars 2, TERA, WildStar, Final Fantasy XIV's collapse and A Realm Reborn, The Elder Scrolls Online, Black Desert, New World and Lost Ark: what each promised, what happened after launch, and how ideas flowed between these games and World of Warcraft, right down to player housing.

  • Bad timing: EverQuest II launched about two weeks before World of Warcraft, and Vanguard two weeks after The Burning Crusade.
  • 2008: Age of Conan shipped a million copies in under three weeks. Warhammer Online sold 1.2 million and then fell to about 300,000 subscribers, closing in December 2013.
  • Rift: Scott Hartsman's account of the "We're not in Azeroth anymore" campaign, the one-word reply from Blizzard, and why the second year mattered more than launch.
  • Star Wars: The Old Republic: 1 million subscribers in three days, 1.7 million by January 2012, free-to-play within the year.
  • Guild Wars 2: The 2010 manifesto, dynamic events and a subscription-free model; over 2 million sold by September 2012.
  • WildStar and TERA: A studio founded by World of Warcraft veterans that closed in 2018, and a decade of action combat that ended in 2022.
  • Final Fantasy XIV: The 2010 disaster, Naoki Yoshida's rebuild after studying World of Warcraft, A Realm Reborn (August 2013), the 2021 surge and the Endwalker sales pause.
  • New business models: The Elder Scrolls Online's Tamriel Unlimited, Black Desert's buy-to-play launch, and the Steam-era peaks of New World and Lost Ark.

title: Azeroth Unearthed, Part 10: Forever and Beyond
summary_html:
The Season One finale of Azeroth Unearthed traces the road from the Nostalrius private server to World of Warcraft Classic, through Season of Mastery, Hardcore, Season of Discovery and the anniversary realms, to World of Warcraft: Forever, which launched on November 4, 2026. Alder and Pip cover what Forever changes, how its first eleven days went, the Worldsoul Saga in the modern game, what little is known about The Last Titan, and Glurp Glurp's road ahead. Note: we could not verify the details of the Turtle WoW legal case from reliable sources in time for this episode, so we flag it on air and do not describe its claims or outcome.

  • Nostalrius: opened February 2015, 800,000+ accounts, shut down by cease and desist on April 10, 2016; the petition, the 80-page post-mortem, and Elysium.
  • Classic: announced at BlizzCon on November 3, 2017, launched August 2019 with a million Twitch viewers, layering, and Golden Joystick PC Game of the Year.
  • The experiments: Season of Mastery (2021), official Hardcore (August 2023) and Self-Found, Season of Discovery (November 2023 to May 2025), and the 20th Anniversary realms moving into The Burning Crusade in February 2026.
  • Private servers and Turtle: Blizzard's history of legal action (Glider, gold sellers, Nostalrius), and an honest flag on the unverified Turtle case.
  • Forever's design: a separate vanilla-era timeline, level 60 forever, three new zones, 1,000+ quests, nine dungeons, 10 and 20 player raids, the Skyborne, Forsaken paladins and Dwarf shamans.
  • Forever's systems: realmless play with two-part names, optional transmog, Campfire, weather and day/night, no shared tagging, included with a subscription.
  • Launch and week one: a relatively smooth November 4 launch, the Olympus guild, and the removal of level 60 quest gold plus the November 11 hotfixes.
  • Worldsoul Saga: The War Within, Midnight (March 2, 2026), Patch 12.2 Eclipse, and The Last Titan's return to Northrend, with details due in early 2027.
  • Classic vs. Forever: a side-by-side for players deciding where to play.
  • For Glurp Glurp: pacing toward the December 9 raids, gold planning, detours, and raptor avoidance.

title: The Expansions, Part 8: Shadowlands
summary_html:
Part Eight of The Expansions covers Shadowlands (2020): the BlizzCon 2019 reveal, Sylvanas shattering the Helm of Domination, the level squish and new player experience, a four-week delay, a record first-day launch, Covenants and Torghast, launch reviews versus later player sentiment, Chains of Domination and the Sanctum ending, the July 2021 lawsuit, the covenant loosening in 9.1.5, the Jailer's defeat in Eternity's End, cross-faction play in 9.2.5, and what lasted.

  • Announcement: Revealed with preorders at BlizzCon on November 1, 2019.
  • Pre-patch 9.0.1 (Oct 13, 2020): The game's first level squish (120 to 50, new cap 60), Exile's Reach, Chromie Time campaigns, an expanded barber shop, and the Death Rising event.
  • Delay and launch: Moved from October 27 to November 23, 2020, the game's sixteenth anniversary; Blizzard reported over 3.7 million first-day sales and called it the fastest-selling PC game ever, a claim PC Gamer flagged as heavily caveated.
  • Story: The Maw, Oribos, the dormant Arbiter and the anima drought; Bastion, Maldraxxus, Ardenweald and Revendreth.
  • Systems: Covenants, Soulbinds, Conduits and Renown; Torghast, Soul Ash, the Runecarver and the Tarragrue.
  • Raids and the race: Castle Nathria, Sanctum of Domination and Sepulcher of the First Ones; Echo forms from Method's roster.
  • Reception: Metacritic 83 with strong launch reviews, then a decline in player sentiment over time-gating, end-game systems, content gaps and the story.
  • 2021 lawsuit: The California DFEH suit, the walkout, J. Allen Brack's departure and in-game content changes (covered in depth in Season 1, Part 7).
  • Patches: 9.1 Chains of Domination, 9.1.5 covenant freedom and the Mage Tower's return, 9.2 Eternity's End (tier sets and the Creation Catalyst), and 9.2.5 cross-faction play.
  • Ending: The Jailer's defeat, Anduin breaking Kingsmourne, and Tyrande's sentence for Sylvanas.
